items.stem: Which of the following best describes "blog"?
options: Dividing exam time evenly between texts and stages
A promotional leaflet describing a place, organisation or service
An online journal or series of posts with a personal voice and interactive features
A statement describing the qualities of work at a given level for a criterion
items.answer: An online journal or series of posts with a personal voice and interactive features
items.markingKey: C. "blog" is an online journal or series of posts with a personal voice and interactive features.

items.stem: Briefly explain why Paper 1 students should know the conventions of many text types.
items.answer: Unseen texts can be any type; knowing conventions lets students recognise how the writer uses or subverts them quickly.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Unseen texts can be any type; knowing conventions lets students recognise how the writer uses or subverts them quickly. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Paper 1 only uses common text types such as adverts and speeches." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Paper 1 may use any non-literary text type, including reviews, brochures, blogs, infographics and cartoons.
items.markingKey: Paper 1 may use any non-literary text type, including reviews, brochures, blogs, infographics and cartoons. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a student delegate at an international youth climate summit.

Delegates, I was born in 2008. In my lifetime the sea outside my grandmother's house in Tuvalu has crept forty metres closer. Forty metres. You measure progress in decades; we measure it in doorsteps. You tell us we are the future. But we are not the future – we are the present, standing in water. So do not applaud me. Applause is cheap. Act.

Identify the audience and purpose of this unseen text and support your answer.
items.answer: Adult delegates and policymakers at an international summit, and a wider media audience watching the speech. To challenge leaders to move from symbolic gestures, such as applause for young speakers, to concrete climate action.
items.markingKey: Adult delegates and policymakers at an international summit, and a wider media audience watching the speech. To challenge leaders to move from symbolic gestures, such as applause for young speakers, to concrete climate action. Award marks for an accurate, specific point (criterion A: understanding and interpretation) supported by a reference to the text; a general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Read the following donation page on an animal-rescue charity's website, described in words.

[Photograph: a one-eyed dog looks straight into the camera.]
'Meet Biscuit. He was found tied to a motorway barrier in January.'
Progress bar: 'This month: 8,450 euros of 10,000 raised.'
Buttons: 10 | 25 | 50 | Other. A pre-ticked box: 'Make this a monthly gift'.
Footer: '94 cents of every euro goes directly to animal care.'

Analyse how the phrase "tied to a motorway barrier in January" contributes to the writer's purpose.
items.answer: Emotive detail: "tied to a motorway barrier in January" – specific cruelty and winter cold provoke pity and anger.
items.markingKey: Emotive detail: "tied to a motorway barrier in January" – specific cruelty and winter cold provoke pity and anger. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following editorial cartoon, described in words.

[A pair of scales of justice. On one pan sits a tiny pile of coins labelled 'Fine for polluting the river'. On the other, a mountain of banknotes labelled 'Annual profit'. The scales tip violently towards the profit. A very small judge peers up at it and says: 'Well, that'll teach them.']

Identify the audience and purpose of this unseen text and support your answer.
items.answer: Readers concerned about corporate responsibility and environmental law. To criticise fines that are too small to change the behaviour of large companies.
items.markingKey: Readers concerned about corporate responsibility and environmental law. To criticise fines that are too small to change the behaviour of large companies. Award marks for an accurate, specific point (criterion A: understanding and interpretation) supported by a reference to the text; a general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Knowing text-type conventions is the most important preparation for Paper 1."
items.answer: Conventions are a useful starting point; close analysis of choices earns the marks.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it speeds up recognition; conventions frame analysis. Arguments against: close reading of language matters more; unseen texts often mix types. Supported judgement: Conventions are a useful starting point; close analysis of choices earns the marks.

items.stem: Write a review (about 300 words) of a film adaptation of a novel you know, using the conventions of the review form.
items.answer: Indicative content: rating; summary; evaluation of adaptation choices; recommendation; voice.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: rating; summary; evaluation of adaptation choices; recommendation; voice.

items.stem:
Read the following opinion column in a weekend newspaper.

To scroll or not to scroll: that is the question every teenager answers two hundred times a day. Whether 'tis nobler to endure the slings and arrows of the group chat, or to take arms against a sea of notifications and, by switching off, end them. Most of us, adults included, choose the scroll. Hamlet at least had the excuse of a ghost.

Explain the effect of the punchline "Hamlet at least had the excuse of a ghost." on the reader.
items.answer: Punchline: "Hamlet at least had the excuse of a ghost." – the closing joke deflates modern indecision.
items.markingKey: Punchline: "Hamlet at least had the excuse of a ghost." – the closing joke deflates modern indecision. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Distinguish between an advertisement and a review.
items.answer: A review evaluates a product or work independently (ideally) for readers; an advertisement promotes it on behalf of the producer.
items.markingKey: A review evaluates a product or work independently (ideally) for readers; an advertisement promotes it on behalf of the producer. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.answer: time allocation

items.stem: Freya writes: "In HL Paper 1, students must compare the two texts." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: HL students write two separate analyses; no comparison is required.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why the two Paper 1 analyses should be treated as separate essays.
items.answer: Each is marked out of 20 on its own criteria; comparing the texts is not required and wastes time. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a youth climate movement's manifesto.

WE ARE NOT ASKING.
1. We demand that our city ends approval of new fossil-fuel projects by 2030.
2. We demand climate education in every school, in every subject.
3. We demand a seat at every table where our future is decided.
We are told to be patient. Patience is a luxury for those who will not live with the consequences. Join us.

Analyse the effect of the closing imperative "Join us." in the text.
items.answer: The closing imperative "Join us.": it turns the reader from audience into member.
items.markingKey: The closing imperative "Join us.": it turns the reader from audience into member. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following blog post by a wheelchair user reviewing accessibility at a music festival.

They gave the accessible viewing platform a lovely name: The Sky Deck. It was, in fairness, very close to the sky – up three flights of stairs. I watched the headliner on a stranger's phone from the bottom step. Five stars for irony, festival people. Zero for planning.

Guiding question: How does the writer use humour to criticise the festival?
Write the thesis and two body paragraphs of a timed guided analysis of this text.
items.answer: Thesis: humour lets the writer expose exclusion without asking for pity. (1) Irony of the "Sky Deck" up three flights. (2) Bathos of watching on a stranger's phone. (3) The parody rating addresses organisers directly. Evaluation: brevity and humour make the post shareable, increasing pressure on the festival.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Thesis: humour lets the writer expose exclusion without asking for pity. (1) Irony of the "Sky Deck" up three flights. (2) Bathos of watching on a stranger's phone. (3) The parody rating addresses organisers directly. Evaluation: brevity and humour make the post shareable, increasing pressure on the festival. items.stem: Reflect on a timed HL Paper 1 practice: how did you divide your time, and how would you change your approach?
items.answer: Indicative content: specific timings; effects on quality; concrete changes.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "HL Paper 1".
items.answer: Two guided textual analyses of unseen non-literary passages in 2 hours 15 minutes, 40 marks (35%)

items.answer: SL students choose one of two texts and write one analysis in 1 h 15; HL students write on both texts in 2 h 15. Both carry 35%.

items.answer: For example: 67 minutes per text – 15 reading/annotating/planning, 47 writing, 5 checking; brief pause between texts. Justification.

items.answer: Marks depend on the quality described in the bands; a concise, focused analysis can outscore a long, descriptive one.

items.stem:
Read the following advertisement for a language-learning app, published in an in-flight magazine.

[Image: a grandmother and a teenage boy laugh across a kitchen table in Lisbon; steam rises from two cups.]
She never learned English. He never learned Portuguese. Until now.
Fifteen minutes a day. That's all it takes to turn 'Olá' into a conversation.
Lingo Bridge – because some words can't wait for a translator.
Download free. First month on us.

Guiding question: How does the advertisement use the representation of family to sell a product?
A student writes: "The text uses many techniques to persuade the audience." Moderate this thesis against criterion C and rewrite it for the top band.
items.answer: Thesis: the advertisement sells an app by selling reconnection across generations. (1) The image of facing figures in a warm kitchen enacts the brand metaphor of a bridge. (2) Parallel sentences and the fragment "Until now" create a mini-narrative with the app as the turning point. (3) The low-commitment offer removes barriers. Evaluation: the text idealises language learning, implying fluency is quick, and turns family intimacy into a commercial promise.
items.markingKey: Thesis: the advertisement sells an app by selling reconnection across generations. (1) The image of facing figures in a warm kitchen enacts the brand metaphor of a bridge. (2) Parallel sentences and the fragment "Until now" create a mini-narrative with the app as the turning point. (3) The low-commitment offer removes barriers. Evaluation: the text idealises language learning, implying fluency is quick, and turns family intimacy into a commercial promise. Paper 1 criteria (5 marks each, 20 total). A Understanding and interpretation: grasp of the literal and implied meaning, references well chosen. B Analysis and evaluation: how textual features and authorial choices shape meaning, with evaluation of their effect. C Focus and organisation: a clear line of argument that answers the guiding question (or a chosen focus) and is developed coherently. D Language: clear, precise, varied academic register and accurate terminology. 5 = excellent, 3 = adequate, 1 = minimal.

items.stem: A response offers a perceptive interpretation and detailed analysis but has frequent language errors that sometimes obscure meaning. Estimate marks for B and D.

items.markingKey: For example: B 4, D 2 – strong analysis, but language errors affecting clarity limit D.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Students are able to moderate their own work as accurately as teachers."

items.stem:
Read the following text.

[Image: a glossy fashion-advert layout. A model in a neon crop top poses, smiling, in front of a landfill heaped with clothes.]
WEAR IT ONCE. POST IT. BIN IT.
New season, new you – every week.
*Made by someone paid less in a month than this top costs in a day.
#OutfitOfTheMinute

Identify the text type of the extract above.
items.answer: parody advertisement
items.markingKey: D. It is a parody advertisement: it uses conventions such as imitation of a recognisable genre or brand, exaggerated so that the original is criticised.

items.stem:
Read the following opinion column in an English-language newspaper in Lisbon.

My grandmother's street in Alfama now has eleven bakeries and no neighbours. The bakeries sell pastéis de nata to people who will leave on Sunday; the neighbours who once bought bread there have left for good, priced out by short-term rentals. Tourism, we are told, is our salvation. Perhaps. But a city that sells its every doorway eventually has nothing left to show its visitors except itself, emptied.

Guiding question: How does the writer convey the effects of tourism on a local community?
List what a top-band response for criteria A and B would include for this text.
items.answer: Thesis: the writer uses irony and contrast to show that tourism empties what it sells. (1) The juxtaposition of bakeries and neighbours. (2) The ironic "we are told" and minor sentence "Perhaps." undermine the official story. (3) The doorway metaphor and final "emptied" present the city as stripped of life. Evaluation: persuasive through personal voice, though it gives no data on housing.
items.markingKey: Thesis: the writer uses irony and contrast to show that tourism empties what it sells. (1) The juxtaposition of bakeries and neighbours. (2) The ironic "we are told" and minor sentence "Perhaps." undermine the official story. (3) The doorway metaphor and final "emptied" present the city as stripped of life. items.stem:
Read the following restaurant review on a food blog.

Let's start with the bread, because the bread is the best thing here, and that is not entirely a compliment. The menu promises 'a journey through the Andes'; the journey, sadly, stops at the bread basket. The ceviche was tired, the service brisk to the point of rudeness, and the bill – 58 euros for two – arrived faster than the main course. Two stars. Go for the bread. Leave before the journey.

Explain the effect of the imperative "Go for the bread. Leave before the journey." on the reader.
items.answer: Imperative: "Go for the bread. Leave before the journey." – the closing advice is a memorable punchline.
items.markingKey: Imperative: "Go for the bread. Leave before the journey." – the closing advice is a memorable punchline. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following infographic from an international water charity, described in words.

[Title in bold blue capitals: 'THE WALK'.] [A single dotted line runs right across the page and ends at a small well icon.]
Label beside the line: 'The distance many women and girls in rural areas walk for water each day: up to 6 km.'
Below: '20 litres. That's what she carries back – about the weight of a full suitcase.'
[Bottom panel: a tap icon.] 'A donation of 25 euros helps bring a tap within 15 minutes of her home.'

Guiding question: How does the infographic use visual and verbal features to persuade its audience?
You have about 65 minutes for this text in HL Paper 1. Write your plan (thesis and paragraph outline) in the first 15 minutes.
items.answer: Thesis: the infographic converts statistics into a journey the reader can imagine. (1) The dotted line visualises distance. (2) The suitcase comparison and "she" personalise data. (3) The tap icon and specific donation make the solution feel achievable. Evaluation: effective, but risks representing women only as victims.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Thesis: the infographic converts statistics into a journey the reader can imagine. (1) The dotted line visualises distance. (2) The suitcase comparison and "she" personalise data. (3) The tap icon and specific donation make the solution feel achievable. Evaluation: effective, but risks representing women only as victims. Read the following speech by a disability-rights activist at a rally outside a parliament.

They say we ask for special treatment. Ramps are not special. Captions are not special. A lift that works is not special. What is special is a parliament with three hundred steps and not one ramp to its public gallery. We have watched our laws being made from the pavement for long enough. Nothing about us, without us.

How does the writer adapt this text to its audience and purpose?
items.answer: Rally participants, passers-by, journalists and the legislators inside the building. To demand accessible democratic institutions and reject the framing of access as a special privilege.

items.stem:
Read the following opinion column published in a national newspaper.

Let me be clear: I am no technophobe. I file this column from a laptop, on a train, while my phone buzzes like a trapped wasp. But I have watched my own students in Nairobi sit side by side at lunch, heads bowed, in total silence, as if at a funeral. We would never let a casino open in a school corridor. Why, then, do we allow a slot machine in every pocket?

How does the analogy saved for the final sentence shape the reader's experience of the text?
items.answer: The analogy saved for the final sentence: the casino/slot machine comparison lands as a memorable closing punch.
items.markingKey: The analogy saved for the final sentence: the casino/slot machine comparison lands as a memorable closing punch. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a campaigner for women's suffrage at a public meeting in Manchester, 1912 (an original pastiche written for study).

Gentlemen of the press, you call us unreasonable. Very well. Was it reasonable that my mother paid taxes on a shop she ran for thirty years, yet could not vote for the men who spent them? Was it reasonable that the law counted her as a citizen when it came to paying, and as a child when it came to choosing? We have asked politely for forty years. Politeness has been answered with silence. We shall not be silent any longer.

Guiding question: How does the speaker turn the accusation of being "unreasonable" against her opponents?
List what a top-band response for criteria A and B would include for this text.
items.answer: Thesis: the speaker reclaims "reasonable" to argue that the law, not the women, is irrational. (1) The ironic "Very well" accepts the label only to test it. (2) Anaphoric rhetorical questions and the personal example of the mother build a logical case. (3) The antithesis citizen/child exposes legal contradiction; the final vow justifies escalation. Evaluation: addressing the press directly anticipates hostile reporting and frames the meeting's message for a wider public.
items.markingKey: Thesis: the speaker reclaims "reasonable" to argue that the law, not the women, is irrational. (1) The ironic "Very well" accepts the label only to test it. (2) Anaphoric rhetorical questions and the personal example of the mother build a logical case. (3) The antithesis citizen/child exposes legal contradiction; the final vow justifies escalation. Evaluation: addressing the press directly anticipates hostile reporting and frames the meeting's message for a wider public. Paper 1 criteria (5 marks each, 20 total). A Understanding and interpretation: grasp of the literal and implied meaning, references well chosen. B Analysis and evaluation: how textual features and authorial choices shape meaning, with evaluation of their effect. C Focus and organisation: a clear line of argument that answers the guiding question (or a chosen focus) and is developed coherently. D Language: clear, precise, varied academic register and accurate terminology. 5 = excellent, 3 = adequate, 1 = minimal.

items.stem: Noah writes: "Paper 1 only uses common text types such as adverts and speeches." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Paper 1 may use any non-literary text type, including reviews, brochures, blogs, infographics and cartoons.
items.markingKey: Paper 1 may use any non-literary text type, including reviews, brochures, blogs, infographics and cartoons. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following advertisement for a language-learning app, published in an in-flight magazine.

[Image: a grandmother and a teenage boy laugh across a kitchen table in Lisbon; steam rises from two cups.]
She never learned English. He never learned Portuguese. Until now.
Fifteen minutes a day. That's all it takes to turn 'Olá' into a conversation.
Lingo Bridge – because some words can't wait for a translator.
Download free. First month on us.

Guiding question: How does the advertisement use the representation of family to sell a product?
You have about 65 minutes for this text in HL Paper 1. Write your plan (thesis and paragraph outline) in the first 15 minutes.
items.answer: Thesis: the advertisement sells an app by selling reconnection across generations. (1) The image of facing figures in a warm kitchen enacts the brand metaphor of a bridge. (2) Parallel sentences and the fragment "Until now" create a mini-narrative with the app as the turning point. (3) The low-commitment offer removes barriers. Evaluation: the text idealises language learning, implying fluency is quick, and turns family intimacy into a commercial promise.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Thesis: the advertisement sells an app by selling reconnection across generations. (1) The image of facing figures in a warm kitchen enacts the brand metaphor of a bridge. (2) Parallel sentences and the fragment "Until now" create a mini-narrative with the app as the turning point. (3) The low-commitment offer removes barriers. Evaluation: the text idealises language learning, implying fluency is quick, and turns family intimacy into a commercial promise. Markbands (criteria A–D). A Knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B Analysis and evaluation of authorial choices; C Focus and organisation; D Language. Top band: an insightful, convincing interpretation supported by well-chosen references; perceptive analysis of how specific choices shape meaning and affect the audience; a sustained, coherent line of argument; precise, varied, register-appropriate academic language. Middle band: relevant interpretation and some analysis, but partly descriptive or unevenly supported. Low band: mostly summary or feature-spotting without effect.

items.stem:
Read the following three-panel comic strip, described in words.

[Panel 1: a world leader at a podium declares, 'We pledge to reach net zero by 2050!' Applause lines fill the background.]
[Panel 2: a polar bear on a shrinking ice floe raises a paw: 'Question – what's the plan for this summer?']
[Panel 3: the leader, sweating, looks away: 'Next question.']

Guiding question: How does the comic strip criticise political responses to climate change?
List what a top-band response for criteria A and B would include for this text.
items.answer: Thesis: the strip contrasts distant promises with present danger. (1) Pledge and applause as performance. (2) The bear as questioner. (3) Evasion as punchline. Evaluation: effective simplification, though it treats all pledges as empty.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Knowing text-type conventions is the most important preparation for Paper 1."
items.answer: Conventions are a useful starting point; close analysis of choices earns the marks.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it speeds up recognition; conventions frame analysis. Arguments against: close reading of language matters more; unseen texts often mix types. Supported judgement: Conventions are a useful starting point; close analysis of choices earns the marks.

items.stem: "It is better to write two solid analyses than one brilliant and one weak." Discuss.
items.answer: Balance is usually safer: consistent quality across both maximises the total.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: each is worth 20 marks; a very weak second response loses many marks. Arguments against: an excellent response may earn more marks overall if the other is adequate; strengths vary. items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Students are able to moderate their own work as accurately as teachers."
items.answer: With practice and benchmarks students get closer, but teacher moderation remains more reliable.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: clear descriptors help; practice improves accuracy. Arguments against: students tend to over- or under-mark; expertise in standards takes time.
